did_you_know.text: The chapter begins by recalling the death of Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu in chapter 10. Their death explains why entering the holy place requires special care.
The parokhet was the curtain separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, while the kapporet was the cover of the Ark of the Covenant.
On Yom Kippur, the high priest wore simple linen garments instead of his usual splendid clothing. The Sages understood this as a form of modest and humble dress.
The word “Azazel” appears only in this chapter, and its exact meaning is debated. It has been understood both as the name of a wilderness place and as a term connected with sending the goat away.
“Incense of spices” was a mixture of fragrant substances, not ordinary smoke. Burning it created a cloud inside the sanctuary.
In the Temple service, “sprinkling” meant flicking or applying blood, usually with a finger. It was a technical term used in purification rituals.
The chapter presents impurity not only as a condition of a person, but also as something that can affect the sacred space among the people.
The phrase “a man appointed for the task” probably describes someone specially prepared or chosen for the job, not the man’s personal name.
The tenth day of the seventh month is the tenth of Tishrei in the Hebrew calendar used today. The Sages understood “you shall afflict yourselves” mainly as fasting and avoiding certain pleasures.
The phrase “Sabbath of complete rest” strongly emphasizes total rest. This is why Jewish tradition treats Yom Kippur as a day of rest with a status resembling Shabbat.
The service described here was not a daily ritual but an annual one, allowing the entire community to begin a new cycle of purification and renewal.
